specPoints.text: describe the difference between contamination and irradiation

primer.text: Two words, one trap. Irradiation bathes an object in radiation from outside — the object never becomes radioactive. Contamination puts radioactive atoms onto or into the material itself — and then it is radioactive. Protection differs for each, and the exam tests the difference.

lessons.title: Contamination versus irradiation
lessons.opening: Contamination is the unwanted arrival of radioactive material on or inside a substance — an accident, such as a leak — and the material becomes radioactive as a result. Irradiation is the deliberate exposure of a material to ionising radiation: useful for sterilisation, and it never makes the material radioactive.
keyPoints: Contamination is the unwanted transfer of radioactive material onto or into something.
A contaminated object becomes radioactive because it now contains a source.
Irradiation is exposing a material to ionising radiation, usually deliberately.
Irradiation does not make the exposed object radioactive.
Irradiation can still kill living cells — sterility comes at a dose.

low.restatement: Spill isotope on the bench: contaminated. Shine gamma at the bench: irradiated, but wipe-clean ordinary matter either way.
low.analogy: Contamination is spilling paint ON you; irradiation is standing in the spray of a paint gun — wet paint only where it lands as matter.
low.examPointer: The money sentence: only contamination makes things radioactive — irradiation never does.

medium.restatement: The distinction is about location of the source: outside the object (irradiation) versus part of the object (contamination). Consequences follow: irradiation stops when the beam stops, contamination persists and emits until the isotope decays or is removed.
medium.analogy: Sunlight warms you only while you stand in it (irradiation); a charcoal briquette in your pocket keeps burning wherever you go (contamination).
medium.examPointer: Comparison tables on this pair are frequent — rehearse description/source/prevention/causes rows.

check.stem: Which process can make an object radioactive?

options.explanation: Only containing radioactive atoms makes an object radioactive.
Exposure to radiation does not create a source.
The asymmetry is the entire point.

check.stem: Irradiating a surgical instrument makes it…

options.explanation: The dose kills organisms; no atoms are transferred.

options.text: an accident or mistake, such as a leak

check.stem: A worker stands near a gamma source behind a screen. If a spot of the source’s dust lands on their sleeve, the worker is now…

options.text: both irradiated (by the source) and contaminated (by the dust)
options.explanation: Exposure from the source plus transferred atoms.

options.text: neither, because a screen was present
options.explanation: The screen does not undo either process.

check.stem: Why does an irradiated object stop posing a radiation risk as soon as it leaves the beam?

options.text: because it contains no source of its own — the radiation came from outside

options.explanation: Absorption is not retention of a source.

options.text: because the beam ionises the air instead
options.explanation: Air ionisation is irrelevant to the object.

check.modelAnswer: Contamination is the unwanted, accidental transfer of radioactive material onto or into some object, which then becomes radioactive itself.
Irradiation means deliberately exposing a material to ionising radiation — and the material does not become radioactive as a result.

check.stem: Explain why a contaminated object remains dangerous long after the spill, while an irradiated one does not.
check.modelAnswer: The contaminated object carries its own radioactive source, which keeps emitting until the isotope decays or is removed; the irradiated object holds no source, so the risk ends when the exposure does.

check.stem: A sealed syringe is gamma-irradiated, and later a drop of radioactive solution splashes onto a second syringe. Contrast the two syringes’ states.
check.modelAnswer: The first is sterile and not radioactive — irradiation transferred no atoms; the second is contaminated — it carries radioactive material and emits radiation until cleaned or decayed.

lessons.title: Protection and the comparison
lessons.opening: Irradiation risk falls with time, distance and shielding; contamination risk falls with airtight barriers and careful handling, because blocking an internal emitter is impossible. Inside the body, contamination is the graver hazard — the source rides with you.
keyPoints: Irradiation exposure is reduced by minimising time and maximising distance from the source.
Contamination is prevented by airtight suits and safe handling, not by shielding after the fact.
Inhaled or ingested sources — radon gas, contaminated food — irradiate the internal organs from inside.
Contamination is generally the greater risk; irradiation is usually deliberate and controlled.
Long-half-life sources pose the greater contamination risk — the long-term burden that waste policy must carry.

low.restatement: Beam hazard: step back, hurry up, hide behind lead. Spill hazard: seal up, gloves on, never touch — you cannot shield what is already inside.
low.analogy: Irradiation is standing near a bonfire — move away. Contamination is a lit match in your pocket — distance is no longer available.
low.examPointer: Match each protection to its hazard; swapping them is the classic lost mark.

medium.restatement: The half-life asymmetry explains the risk table: high activity (short half-life) means intense irradiation now, while longevity (long half-life) means a contamination burden that persists for storage lifetimes. Hence waste policy favours long-term geological isolation, and laboratory policy favours tongs and short exposures.
medium.analogy: A short-half-life source is a firework — fierce but brief; a long-half-life source is a slow candle — gentle but it stays lit for years.
medium.examPointer: WE-style questions ask for the half-life risk split: short → irradiation, long → contamination.

check.stem: Which practice reduces irradiation from an external source?

options.text: maximising distance and minimising exposure time
options.explanation: Distance and time are the irradiation levers.

check.stem: What is the point of an airtight suit in a contaminated area?

options.text: it stops radioactive atoms getting onto or into the worker
options.explanation: The suit is the barrier against transfer.

options.text: it shields the worker from gamma rays
options.explanation: A suit is not gamma shielding.

options.text: it makes the worker immune to irradiation
it cleans the air of radiation

check.stem: Why is inhaled radon particularly hazardous?

options.text: it is a contamination route putting an alpha emitter inside the lungs
options.explanation: Internal alpha delivery is the worst case.

options.text: because alpha cannot travel through air
options.explanation: Air travel is exactly how it is inhaled.

options.text: because radon is more penetrating than gamma
because radon irradiates from outside the body

check.stem: A source has a very short half-life. Its chief risk profile is…

options.text: high irradiation risk from intense activity
options.explanation: Short half-life → high activity → strong exposure.
High activity is precisely the risk.

options.text: secure long-term storage to prevent contamination spreading

options.explanation: That is not the named control.

check.stem: State how to reduce the risk from irradiation by an external source.
check.modelAnswer: Minimise the time spent near the source, maximise the distance from it, and use shielding where possible.
Contamination is prevented by handling sources safely — airtight protective clothing, gloves and tongs — so radioactive atoms never transfer onto or into a person.

check.stem: Explain why contamination inside the body is more dangerous than the same activity outside.
check.modelAnswer: Inside the body there is no distance and no shielding; the source directly irradiates internal organs as it moves through them.

check.stem: Summarise the difference in risk between short-half-life and long-half-life sources for (a) irradiation and (b) contamination.
check.modelAnswer: (a) Short half-lives mean high activity, so irradiation risk is greatest for them. (b) Long half-lives remain radioactive for longer, so contamination risk persists and demands long-term control and storage.

glossary.definition: The accidental transfer of a radioactive substance onto or into a material.
Exposing a material to ionising radiation without it becoming radioactive.
Protective clothing that prevents radioactive atoms reaching the skin or being inhaled.
Short half-lives dominate irradiation risk; long half-lives dominate contamination risk.
